newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African labour seeks sweeping economic changes.
newsitem.headline: S.African labour seeks sweeping economic changes.

text.p: Leaders of South Africa's labour movement have called for sweeping economic changes to eradicate the economic legacy of apartheid, which still sees most of the country's wealth in white hands.

Among the steps sought by Cosatu, the country's largest labour federation, is a policy of lowering interest rates, restructuring the central Reserve Bank, wage cuts on higher salaried-people and punitive taxes to discourage speculation.
"It would represent the most serious concrete challenge by the democratic forces to the relations of economic power in the country," Cosatu said in a discussion document.

The federation and the South African Communist Party are political allies with the ruling African National Congress (ANC), but the government has rolled back on socialist-sounding promises dating from the days Nelson Mandela was in jail and his then-banned ANC was based in exile.

Mandela's government is increasingly at odds with its former allies on the left who have condemned what they see as a shift to "neo-liberalism", including plans to privatise state corporations and rein in public spending.

The ANC launched its flagship Reconstruction and Development Programme to eradicate the disparities between blacks and whites after decades of apartheid once it took power in the country's first all-race elections in April 1994.
Initial reverses and slow progress led to the plan being farmed out to government ministries.
The 1.5 million member Cosatu wants to resurrect the programme and is proposing that its rank and file approve a new package to redistribute wealth and reduce inequality.

"A flattening of the wage and salary structure between the top and the bottom would represent a massive gain for economic redistribution, and reduction of inequality, given the size of the gap we have inherited," the document says.

Cosatu proposes that any "social accord" aimed at economic growth would need to "reorganise the wage structure and raise the living standards of the majority of workers. This may entail restraints or cuts for the high-paid, including management."
The plan would also include a national training levy and a national compulsory pension fund.

Cosatu leaders also have speculators in their sights and part of the fight against "hot money" which has hammered the rand over the past year would include action on South Africa's interest rates -- among the world's highest in real terms.
"There should be a deliberate policy of lowering interest rates," the document says.
"High interest rates and lack of commitment to economic development have resulted in hot, speculative investment."
